analysis.one_liner: Strips the EPA's power to override state water pollution decisions and speeds discharge permits.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 239-184 in July 2011, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop the Environmental Protection Agency from overruling a state's water quality standards, its permitting decisions, or its approval of discharges into rivers, lakes, and coastal waters. It would also cut the time federal agencies get to review dredge-and-fill permits to 30 days and require EPA to publish a state-by-state jobs analysis before new water rules. In practice, a state could keep weaker pollution standards than EPA believes the Clean Water Act requires, and EPA could not veto a state-issued permit it thought would harm drinking water, shellfish beds, or fisheries.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries that discharge pollution into water — mining companies (especially mountaintop-removal coal), industrial plants, large farms, and developers filling wetlands — would face a weaker federal backstop and faster permits. State governors and legislatures gain final say over water standards, with EPA unable to step in when it disagrees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Mining, industrial and farm polluters, developers

how_it_helps.text: Bars the EPA from issuing a stricter water quality standard for a pollutant if the state disagrees, effectively giving states the final word once EPA has approved their standard once [S2].

Prohibits EPA from superseding a state's decision that a discharge complies with pollution limits, and from objecting to state-issued discharge permits based on disagreement over how a standard is implemented [S2].
Blocks EPA from designating an area off-limits for dredged or fill material disposal if the state where the discharge originates does not concur [S2].
Shortens the comment deadline for federal agencies reviewing dredge-and-fill permits from 90 days to 30 days (or 60 if extended), speeding projects along [S5].

analysis.who_pays: People who drink, fish, and swim in the affected waters. If a state keeps a weak standard or issues a permit EPA disagrees with, downstream communities, drinking water systems, shellfisheries, and recreational economies absorb the pollution, and public water systems pay more to treat dirtier source water.
analysis.who_pays_short: People who drink and use affected waters

drawbacks.text: A state that has already had a standard approved could keep it even if EPA later determines it does not meet the Clean Water Act's requirements, leaving no federal backstop for weaker state protections [S2].
The bill's 30-day deadline for agency comments gives reviewers far less time to evaluate the environmental risks of dredge-and-fill permits than the current 90 days [S5].

The required jobs analysis counts job losses but explicitly bars counting offsetting job gains from new technologies or government employment, structuring the analysis toward finding negative impacts [S5].
The bill's annual report on waterborne pathogens, toxic chemicals, and metals (Section 6) is monitoring only — it documents changes in pollution without any authority to act on them [S4].

For states and permit applicants, the counterargument is real: the current system lets EPA override state decisions years after the fact, creating uncertainty for projects and jobs, and states bear day-to-day responsibility for their own waters.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — faster permits and more state control — flow mainly to the industries seeking to discharge or fill, while the cost of weaker federal oversight falls on the public's water. The bill adds a pollutant-monitoring report, but reporting is not protection: the same bill removes the tools (stricter standards, permit vetoes) that would fix problems the report might find. Its central design flaw is that a state's one-time approval of a standard becomes permanent, with no federal remedy if the state then implements it loosely.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House in July 2011, was placed on the Senate calendar a few days later, and never came up for a vote before that Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Introduced May 26, 2011, and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee [S7].
The committee ordered it reported 35-19 on June 22, 2011 [S7].

Before final passage, the House defeated a motion to send the bill back with instructions to preserve EPA's authority over discharges into waters that are sources of public drinking water, 188-238 [S8].
The House passed the bill 239-184 on July 13, 2011, with 223 of 239 Republicans and only 16 of 192 Democrats voting yes [S9].
The Senate received the bill, placed it on its calendar on July 18, 2011, and took no further action for the rest of the 112th Congress [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, EPA kept its authority to set stricter standards, veto state discharge permits, and block fill permits that threaten drinking water, shellfish beds, and fisheries. Communities and public water systems are better off than they would have been under the bill; the mining and discharge interests that sought the change gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was 239-184, with 223 of 239 Republicans and only 16 of 192 Democrats in favor; the motion to recommit to protect drinking-water sources failed almost entirely along party lines, 188-238 [S9] [S8].

industries.note: The bill would bar EPA from vetoing a state-approved dredge-and-fill permit whenever the state concurs, targeting the EPA veto power used against large fill operations such as the Spruce No. 1 mountaintop-removal coal mine in West Virginia earlier in 2011. Mining companies would gain permits that federal review currently can stop; downstream communities would absorb the resulting sediment and water contamination.

EPA could no longer object to state-issued discharge permits based on disagreement over how a state implements its own water quality standard, and could not supersede a state's compliance determination. Polluters in permissive states would face less federal second-guessing of their permits.
Limits on EPA's veto of fill permits plus a shortened 30-day agency comment window would let wetland-filling and construction projects move faster and with less risk of a late-stage federal stop.

With EPA unable to override state decisions on discharges into waters used as drinking water sources, utilities would face dirtier source water and higher treatment costs, a concern opponents raised in the motion to recommit the bill.
